clinicalPearls: Abrupt, often near-total hair loss occurring within days to a few weeks of an insult, in contrast to the delayed shedding of telogen effluvium

Most commonly caused by cytotoxic chemotherapy; other causes include radiotherapy, severe toxin or heavy-metal exposure such as thallium or arsenic, and occasionally severe protein-energy malnutrition
Hairs are lost during the anagen (growing) phase, so shed shafts show tapered or fractured proximal ends rather than the club roots of telogen hairs
Because about ninety per cent of scalp follicles are in anagen at any time, the loss can be dramatic and cosmetically severe
Trichoscopy may show tapering hairs, black dots and broken hairs, and follicular ostia are preserved so the process is non-scarring
Regrowth is expected once the offending agent is withdrawn, although texture or colour may change temporarily, producing the well-recognised post-chemotherapy curls
Scalp cooling during chemotherapy can reduce severity with some regimens; otherwise the mainstay is reassurance and cosmetic support such as wigs
reference.pathophysiology: Anagen effluvium arises when an insult abruptly impairs the rapidly dividing matrix keratinocytes of follicles in the active growth phase. Cytotoxic drugs, ionising radiation and certain poisons arrest mitosis, producing a narrowed, weakened hair shaft that fractures within the follicular canal, so hair is shed while still in anagen and without the latency seen in telogen effluvium. Because the germinative cells are inhibited rather than destroyed and the follicular architecture is preserved, hair regrows once the toxic stimulus is removed, though certain intensive regimens can occasionally cause permanent loss.
additionalDifferentials: Telogen effluvium, which is delayed, less complete and sheds club hairs
Alopecia areata, especially diffuse or totalis forms
Congenital or acquired hair-shaft disorders causing fragility
additionalInvestigations: History of chemotherapy, radiotherapy or toxin exposure
Light microscopy of shed or plucked hairs to identify tapered anagen roots and shaft narrowing
Trichoscopy to detect tapering and broken hairs with preserved ostia
Heavy-metal screening where poisoning is suspected
Scalp biopsy only if the diagnosis is unclear or a scarring process is suspected
redFlags: Failure of regrowth months after the toxin is withdrawn, suggesting permanent chemotherapy-induced alopecia or an alternative diagnosis
Systemic features of heavy-metal poisoning such as neuropathy or gastrointestinal upset
Signs of scarring with loss of ostia indicating a different, irreversible process
reference.prognosis: Regrowth is the rule once the causative agent is stopped, usually beginning within weeks to a few months, although permanent alopecia is increasingly recognised after certain intensive regimens, notably the taxanes.
pitfalls: Confusing the rapid, near-complete loss of anagen effluvium with the slower, partial shedding of telogen effluvium
Overlooking non-chemotherapy causes such as thallium or arsenic poisoning
Failing to warn patients of possible permanent alopecia with high-risk regimens
Assuming any regrowth abnormality is pathological when transient colour and texture change is common
management: Identify and, where possible, withdraw or avoid the causative insult such as a cytotoxic drug or toxin
Offer scalp cooling during chemotherapy to reduce the severity of hair loss
Institute chelation therapy where heavy-metal poisoning such as thallium or arsenic is the cause
Reassure the patient that regrowth is expected once the offending agent is stopped, though texture or colour may change temporarily
Provide camouflage such as wigs and psychological support during the period of alopecia
Remain alert to the possibility of permanent alopecia after certain intensive regimens, notably the taxanes
